slides.text: A variable is a named place that holds a value. Here you declare variables with `var` and with `:=`, see which value they start with, change them, meet two errors Go reports before the program runs, and declare several variables at once.

intro.title: A named box for a value

slides.text:
Think of a variable as a labeled box: a **name**, a **type** that says what can go inside, and a **value**. Go checks the type, so a box for numbers never holds text.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
box age holds a whole number
put 30 in age        ok
put "thirty" in age  error

slides.text: Go has two ways to declare one. `var` is explicit and works everywhere. `:=` is the short form: it works inside functions and takes the type from the value.

exercises.title: Declare with var
exercises.guide: Inside `main`, declare two variables with `var` and print them.

chunks.guide: `var` declares a variable: its name, then its type, then its value.

notes.text: Makes a variable you can change later.
The type goes after the name.

chunks.guide: `int` is a whole number.
`Println` prints its values, separated by a space.

notes.text: Prints each value, separated by a space.

exercises.title: Match the type
exercises.guide: Give `age` a type that holds text.

exercises.title: Zero values
exercises.guide: Declare three variables without a value, then print them.

chunks.guide: Without a value, a variable starts with the **zero value** of its type: 0, empty text or false.

notes.text: With no value, a variable starts at zero.

chunks.text:
var count int
    var name string
    var ok bool

chunks.guide: The empty text prints as nothing, so there are two spaces in the output.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `total` has no value, so it starts as the zero value of `int`, which is 0.

exercises.title: The short form
exercises.guide: Declare two variables with `:=` and print them.

chunks.guide: `:=` declares a variable and takes its type from the value. It only works inside a function.

notes.text: Declares and assigns in one step.

chunks.guide: `2024` is a whole number, so `year` is an `int`.
Print them, as before.

exercises.title: Change a value
exercises.guide: Declare a variable, then change its value.

chunks.guide: Declare `score` once.
To change it later, use `=` with no colon: `score` already exists.
Print the new value.

exercises.title: Reuse a variable
exercises.guide: `level` already exists. Give it the value 5 with a plain assignment.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    level := 1
    level ___ 5
    fmt.Println(level)
}

exercises.title: Swap two values
exercises.guide: Declare two variables and swap them in one line.

chunks.guide: You can declare several variables on one line.

notes.text: Declares two variables in one line.

chunks.guide: Both sides are worked out before the assignment, so this swaps the values.

notes.text: The right side is read first.

chunks.guide: Print them.

exercises.title: What kind of error is it?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the kind of error.
exercises.explanation: Go refuses to compile a variable that is declared and never used.

slides.text: You can declare several variables in one go: group them in a `var ( ... )` block, or put several names on one line.

Go makes you use every variable, so it gives you `_`, the **blank identifier**: a place that takes a value and throws it away.

`:=` has two rules. It needs at least one **new** name on its left side, and it only works inside a function. At the top of a file, use `var`.

exercises.title: Group with var
exercises.guide: Declare three variables in one `var` block, then print them.

chunks.guide: One `var` with parentheses declares many variables, one per line. `admin` has no value, so it starts as false.

notes.text: No need to repeat var on each line.

chunks.guide: Print them.

exercises.title: Complete the block
exercises.guide: Fill the gaps of the grouped declaration.

exercises.title: Several on one line
exercises.guide: Declare several variables per line, then print them.

chunks.guide: Several names can share one type. Both start at 0.

notes.text: Two variables of one type in a single line.

chunks.guide: Assign both in one line, in order.
`:=` also takes several names, and each one gets the type of its own value.
Print all four.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var a, b int
    a, b = 5, a
    fmt.Println(a, b)
}
exercises.explanation: The right side is worked out first, while `a` is still 0. Then `a` becomes 5 and `b` becomes 0.

exercises.title: Ignore a value
exercises.guide: Throw a value away with `_`, and use it to satisfy the compiler.

chunks.guide: `_` is the **blank identifier**. It takes the first value and discards it, so only `score` is kept.
Nothing uses `count` yet, and Go would refuse to compile it.
Assigning it to `_` counts as a use.

notes.text: Counts as a use, so Go does not complain.

chunks.guide: Print the score.

exercises.title: One new variable
exercises.guide: Use `:=` with one old name and one new name.

chunks.guide: Both names are new.
`:=` needs at least one new name on the left. `secure` is new, so `port` is only updated, not redeclared.

notes.text: The one new name that makes := legal.

chunks.guide: Print all three.

exercises.title: Outside a function
exercises.guide: Declare a variable at the top of the file, outside `main`.

chunks.guide: Outside a function, every declaration starts with `var`. The short form `:=` only works inside functions.

notes.text: The type is worked out from the value.

chunks.guide: Inside `main`, `:=` is fine.
Print both.
